name: Liver / organ meats (beef liver)

lead: Beef liver is the organ of a cow, eaten in many cuisines. It is unusually rich in vitamin A, vitamin B12, riboflavin, copper and iron, and in looksmaxxing and ancestral-diet circles it is promoted as a whole-food alternative to multivitamins for skin, energy and general vitality.

No published human trial has tested liver consumption for skin, facial appearance or attractiveness. The nutritional content itself is well documented; the appearance claims are an extension of that content rather than something studied directly.

paras: Proponents reason that nutrients concentrated in liver, especially preformed vitamin A, B vitamins and heme iron, support skin, hair and energy, so eating liver should improve them. The nutrient levels are measured facts; whether eating liver changes appearance in people who are not deficient has not been tested.

Liver contains preformed vitamin A, and reference sources note that a single serving can exceed the adult tolerable upper intake level of 3,000 micrograms per day. Excess preformed vitamin A is associated with headaches, liver damage, bone effects and, in pregnancy, harm to the fetus. Raw liver carries the food-safety concerns associated with any raw meat, and forum members dispute whether it should be eaten raw, frozen or cooked.

lead: Liver is the organ most often meant by the term organ meats or offal in looksmaxxing and ancestral-diet communities. Beef liver in particular is promoted online as a very concentrated food, rich in preformed vitamin A, vitamin B12, riboflavin, copper and iron, and is described by some forum users as nature's multivitamin [1][2].

Reference sources confirm that liver is unusually nutrient-dense and that its vitamin A content is high enough that one slice of beef liver can exceed the adult tolerable upper intake level of 3,000 micrograms of preformed vitamin A per day [3][4]. The same sources document vitamin A poisoning from liver, historically from polar bear, seal and husky livers, and advise caution in pregnancy [3][4].

No published trial has tested whether eating liver changes skin quality, facial appearance or attractiveness. The appearance claims on forums rest on the food's nutrient profile and on personal reports.

paras: Liver is eaten in cuisines around the world, from British liver and onions to Middle Eastern raw liver dishes, and sits within the broader category of offal or organ meats [3][5]. The word offal derives from Germanic roots referring to the parts that fall off in butchering, and organ meats were historically a food of poorer households in places such as medieval England and 18th and 19th century Ireland [5]. Consumption of offal has been reported to rise as people become aware of its nutritional content [5].

Liver is a source of protein and of several micronutrients in high concentration. Wikipedia's nutrition table for raw pork liver lists about 6,500 micrograms of vitamin A (722 percent of the daily value), 26 micrograms of vitamin B12, 3 mg of riboflavin and 23 mg of iron per 100 g, and notes that content varies by species [3]. A looksmax.org thread promoting beef liver lists similar or higher figures for vitamin A, B12 and copper in beef liver and reasons that these concentrations make liver superior to a multivitamin [1].
Liver's B12 content is noted to have helped lead to the discovery of that vitamin [3].

Hypervitaminosis A results from excess preformed vitamin A (retinol and retinyl esters), not from carotenoids such as beta-carotene. Liver is described as a major dietary source [4]. The tolerable upper intake level for adults aged 19 to 70 is listed as 3,000 micrograms per day, and a single 68 g slice of beef liver is cited as containing about 6,410 micrograms [3][4].

Reported symptoms of vitamin A excess include headache, nausea, dizziness, dry and peeling skin, hair loss and increased sun sensitivity. Serious effects include liver damage, high blood calcium and raised pressure within the skull [4]. Excess vitamin A is also reported to shift bone turnover toward resorption, with bone loss and fractures described in the literature [4]. Wikipedia states that excess vitamin A can harm babies whose mothers consumed too much, and it limits intake advice during pregnancy [3][4].

Historical vitamin A poisonings from the livers of polar bears, walruses, bearded seals and huskies are documented, including a 1597 account by Gerrit de Veer and the 1913 deaths associated with Mawson and Mertz's Antarctic expedition, although the latter explanation has been contested [3][4]. Other species carry other hazards, such as mercury in ringed seal liver [3].

Raw meat in general carries food-safety concerns. Raw liver is eaten in some cuisines [3], and forum members disagree about whether liver should be eaten raw, frozen or cooked. One looksmax.org poster insists it must be raw and unfrozen, while others say they eat it in both states or find it unpalatable raw [1][2][6].

On looksmax.org, beef liver is the subject of long guides that present it as the most nutrient-dense whole food, with sections on sourcing, preparation, comparison with multivitamins and special cases such as iron deficiency and cognition [1]. Other threads cover how to cook it, whether goat liver differs from beef liver, and how to make it palatable [2][6][7].

Users commonly report that taste is the main barrier, and some recommend sourcing from grass-fed animals on the basis that such liver tastes milder [6]. The claims centre on skin clarity, energy, hair and testosterone-adjacent vitality, but none of these has been tested specifically for liver in published trials.

No studies found. No published human trial has tested liver or organ-meat consumption for skin condition, facial appearance or attractiveness. The nutritional composition of liver and the effects of excess vitamin A are described in reference sources [3][4], but these are not studies of appearance outcomes.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, beef liver is promoted as a dense whole-food supplement for skin and vitality, and debate centres on whether to eat it raw or cooked [1][2][6].

claims.claim: Beef liver is 'the most powerful food on earth' and outperforms multivitamins.
Raw, unfrozen liver is the best form and cooking or freezing ruins its value.
Eating liver improves skin and general vitality because of its vitamin A and B vitamins.
Vitamin A toxicity from liver is exaggerated.

timeline.event: Gerrit de Veer records severe illness in his crew after eating polar bear liver, an early account of vitamin A poisoning [4].
Douglas Mawson and Xavier Mertz are reported to have been poisoned by eating husky livers on an Antarctic expedition, an explanation that has been contested [3][4].
